summary.text: Cosine-moment formulas for the trinomial factors and the weighted central-binomial generating function convert the series into a double integral of \((840840-1778P)/(P\sqrt P)\), where \(P=273-17\cos x-56\cos y-8\cos x\cos y\). A rational divergence decomposition reduces this integral to a boundary flux; isolating and explicitly integrating the singular cosine kernel as \(\cos x\to-1\), while uniformly bounding the regular remainder, gives the boundary value \(5005\pi/\sqrt{338}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_n(b,c)=[z^n](z^2+bz+c)^n
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}
 \binom nj\binom{n-j}{j}b^{n-2j}c^j.
\]
We prove that, for
\[
t_n=\frac{4290n+367}{3136^n}\binom{2n}{n}T_n(14,1)T_n(17,16),
\]
one has
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t_n=\frac{5390}{\pi}.
\]

The proof has three parts. First we turn the series into a double integral. Second, an explicit rational divergence identity turns that double integral into a boundary integral. Finally we evaluate the limiting boundary integral by isolating its single singular kernel.

## 1. Cosine moments and the binomial generating function

We begin with two standard cosine moments. For every integer \(m\geq 0\),
\[
\int_0^\pi \cos^{2m}x\,dx
 =\pi\frac{\binom{2m}{m}}{4^m},
\qquad
\int_0^\pi \cos^{2m+1}x\,dx=0.                    \tag{1}
\]
For completeness, the odd formula follows either from the substitution \(x\mapsto\pi-x\), or by the usual reduction formula. The even formula follows by induction from integration by parts:
\[
\int_0^\pi\cos^{2m+2}x\,dx
 =\frac{2m+1}{2m+2}\int_0^\pi\cos^{2m}x\,dx,
\]
together with
\[
(m+1)\binom{2m+2}{m+1}=2(2m+1)\binom{2m}{m}.
\]

Expanding a power by the binomial theorem and then applying (1) gives the following useful realization of the generalized trinomial coefficient. If \(b,d\) are integers, then
\[
\int_0^\pi (b+2d\cos x)^n\,dx=\pi T_n(b,d^2).       \tag{2}
\]
Indeed,
\[
(b+2d\cos x)^n
 =\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj b^{n-j}(2d)^j\cos^j x.
\]
All odd terms integrate to zero. In the term \(j=2i\), formula (1) gives
\[
\binom n{2i}b^{n-2i}(2d)^{2i}
 \pi\frac{\binom{2i}{i}}{4^i}
 =\pi\binom ni\binom{n-i}{i}b^{n-2i}d^{2i},
\]
where
\[
\binom n{2i}\binom{2i}{i}=\binom ni\binom{n-i}{i}.
\]
Summing over \(0\leq i\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) proves (2).

We shall also use the central-binomial generating function
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}z^n
 =\frac1{\sqrt{1-z}},\qquad |z|<1.                 \tag{3}
\]
This is the binomial expansion of \((1-z)^{-1/2}\). Differentiating it inside its disk of convergence, or equivalently applying the binomial expansion of \((1-z)^{-3/2}\), yields
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty(4290n+367)
 \frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}z^n
 =\frac{2145-1778(1-z)}{(1-z)\sqrt{1-z}}.          \tag{4}
\]
To see the constants directly, if \(F(z)=(1-z)^{-1/2}\), the left side is
\(4290zF'(z)+367F(z)\), hence its numerator over \((1-z)^{3/2}\) is
\[
2145z+367(1-z)=367+1778z=2145-1778(1-z).
\]

## 2. Conversion of the series to a double integral

Put
\[
P(u,v)=273-17u-56v-8uv,
\qquad
N(u,v)=840840-1778P(u,v),                           \tag{5}
\]
and, for real \(x,y\), put
\[
X(x,y)=\frac{(14+2\cos x)(17+8\cos y)}{784},
\]
\[
I(x,y)=\frac{N(\cos x,\cos y)}
 {P(\cos x,\cos y)\sqrt{P(\cos x,\cos y)}}.       \tag{6}
\]
For \(-1\leq u,v\leq1\),
\[
12\leq14+2u\leq16,
\qquad 9\leq17+8v\leq25.
\]
Consequently
\[
108\leq(14+2u)(17+8v)\leq400,                      \tag{7}
\]
and therefore
\[
0\leq X(x,y)\leq\frac{400}{784}=\frac{25}{49}<1.  \tag{8}
\]
A direct expansion also gives
\[
1-X(x,y)=\frac{P(\cos x,\cos y)}{392}.             \tag{9}
\]
From (7), or directly from (9), one obtains the uniform bounds
\[
192\leq P(u,v)\leq338\qquad(-1\leq u,v\leq1).      \tag{10}
\]
In particular all square roots and denominators in (6) are harmless.

Define
\[
W_n(x,y)=(4290n+367)\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}X(x,y)^n.
\]
Substituting (9) into (4), and noting that \(2145\cdot392=840840\), gives
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty W_n(x,y)=\sqrt{392}\,I(x,y).     \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, the right side of (4), after replacing \(1-X\) by \(P/392\), is
\[
\frac{2145-1778P/392}{(P/392)\sqrt{P/392}}
 =\sqrt{392}\frac{840840-1778P}{P\sqrt P}.
\]

All subsequent exchanges of sum and integral are justified uniformly. Namely,
\[
0\leq\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n}\leq1
\]
and (8) imply
\[
|W_n(x,y)|\leq(4290n+367)\left(\frac{25}{49}\right)^n.   \tag{12}
\]
The majorant is summable, being a linear polynomial in \(n\) times a geometric sequence of ratio \(25/49\). Thus (11) may be integrated twice term by term.

Using (2), first with \((b,d)=(17,4)\) and then with \((b,d)=(14,1)\), we calculate
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^\pi\!\int_0^\pi W_n(x,y)\,dy\,dx
&=(4290n+367)\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{4^n784^n}
  \left(\int_0^\pi(14+2\cos x)^n\,dx\right)
  \left(\int_0^\pi(17+8\cos y)^n\,dy\right)\\
&=\pi^2\frac{4290n+367}{3136^n}\binom{2n}{n}
 T_n(14,1)T_n(17,16)\\
&=\pi^2t_n,
\end{aligned}                                                   \tag{13}
\]
since \(4\cdot784=3136\). Integrating (11), applying (12), and using (13), we obtain
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\sum_{n=0}^\infty t_n
 =\frac{\sqrt{392}}{\pi^2}
   \int_0^\pi\!\int_0^\pi I(x,y)\,dy\,dx.}        \tag{14}
\]
It remains to evaluate the double integral.

## 3. An explicit divergence identity

We now give the rational certificate used for the integral. Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_1(u,v)&=uv-u-v-3,\\
r_2(u,v)&=8u^2v+17u^2+48uv+222u-56v+785,\\
r_4(u,v)&=u^2+48uv-2u-48v+577,
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{15}
\]
and define \(A(u,v)\) by the partial-fraction expression
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(u,v)={}&-
 \frac{7(u-49)(u-25)(u+23)}{2(u-1)r_4(u,v)}
 +\frac{7u-2891}{2u-2}\\
&-\frac{1470(3u+29)(5u+27)}{(u-1)r_2(u,v)}
 +\frac{770(5u-21)}{(u-1)r_1(u,v)}.               \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
Define \(B(u,v)=b(u,v)/(r_1r_2r_4)\), where
\[
\begin{aligned}
b(u,v)=7\big(&192u^5v^2-1984u^5v-5083u^5
 -113856u^4v^2-244576u^4v-5593u^4\\
&-787584u^3v^2-2434560u^3v-2247566u^3
 +4309632u^2v^2-5082176u^2v-13447090u^2\\
&-5802048uv^2+82058944uv+56933561u
 +2393664v^2-74295648v+549185595\big).             \tag{17}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here and below \(r_1r_2r_4\) means the product of the three expressions at \((u,v)\).

Direct differentiation and collection of terms over the common denominator \((r_1r_2r_4)^2\) gives the rational identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\big((1-u^2)P A_u-uPA-\tfrac12(1-u^2)P_uA\big)\\
&\quad+\big((1-v^2)P B_v-vPB-\tfrac12(1-v^2)P_vB\big)=N,         \tag{18}
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
P_u=-17-8v,\qquad P_v=-56-8u.                                  \tag{19}
\]
This is a polynomial identity after denominators are cleared: substitute (5), (15), (16), and (17), multiply by \((r_1r_2r_4)^2\), differentiate the displayed polynomials, and like powers of \(u,v\) cancel, leaving \(N(r_1r_2r_4)^2\). Thus (18) holds wherever the denominators do not vanish.

We record why those denominators do not vanish on the rectangles where we use (18). If \(-1\leq u,v\leq1\), direct rearrangement and elementary inequalities give
\[
r_2(u,v)\geq484,
\qquad r_4(u,v)\geq484.                                      \tag{20}
\]
For example, these bounds follow by completing the relevant squares and using
\((1-u)(u+7)(1-v)\geq0\), \(5u+27\geq22\) for \(r_2\), and
\((1-u)(1-v)\geq0\), \(u+23\geq22\) for \(r_4\).
Moreover, if \(-1<u\leq1\) and \(-1\leq v\leq1\), then
\[
r_1(u,v)<0.                                                   \tag{21}
\]
Indeed, \((1-u)(v+1)\geq0\), and
\[
r_1(u,v)=-(u+3+(1-u)v);
\]
the right-hand parenthesis is positive when \(u>-1\). Hence all rational functions above are smooth when \(-1<u<1\), \(-1\leq v\leq1\).

Set
\[
\Phi_U(x,y)=-\frac{A(\cos x,\cos y)\sin x}
 {\sqrt{P(\cos x,\cos y)}},
\qquad
\Phi_V(x,y)=-\frac{B(\cos x,\cos y)\sin y}
 {\sqrt{P(\cos x,\cos y)}}.                                  \tag{22}
\]
The chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial\Phi_U}{\partial x}
 =\frac{(1-u^2)PA_u-uPA-\frac12(1-u^2)P_uA}{P\sqrt P},
\quad u=\cos x,\ v=\cos y,                                  \tag{23}
\]
and similarly
\[
\frac{\partial\Phi_V}{\partial y}
 =\frac{(1-v^2)PB_v-vPB-\frac12(1-v^2)P_vB}{P\sqrt P}.         \tag{24}
\]
For instance, (23) follows by differentiating
\(-A(u,v)\sin x\,P(u,v)^{-1/2}\), using \(u'=-\sin x\),
\(\sin^2x=1-u^2\), and \((P^{-1/2})'=-(1/2)P^{-3/2}P_u u'\).
Combining (18), (23), and (24), we obtain
\[
I(x,y)=\frac{\partial\Phi_U}{\partial x}(x,y)
       +\frac{\partial\Phi_V}{\partial y}(x,y)                \tag{25}
\]
whenever \(0\leq x<\pi\), \(0\leq y\leq\pi\).

Fix \(0\leq a<\pi\) and integrate (25) over
\([0,a]\times[0,\pi]\). All functions are continuous and smooth there by (10), (20), and (21), so Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus apply. The \(y\)-boundary terms vanish because \(\sin0=\sin\pi=0\), and the \(x=0\) term also vanishes. Therefore
\[
\int_0^a\!\int_0^\pi I(x,y)\,dy\,dx
 =\int_0^\pi\Phi_U(a,y)\,dy.                                  \tag{26}
\]
The difficulty is that the certificate has a singularity at the corner reached as \(a\uparrow\pi\). We next evaluate precisely the limiting flux.

## 4. Isolation and evaluation of the boundary singularity

For \(-1<u<0\), define
\[
D(u,v)=u+3+(1-u)v,
\qquad
K(u)=\frac{770(5u-21)}{u-1},                                  \tag{27}
\]
and let
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(u,v)={}&-
 \frac{7(u-49)(u-25)(u+23)}{2(u-1)r_4(u,v)}
 +\frac{7u-2891}{2u-2}\\
&-\frac{1470(3u+29)(5u+27)}{(u-1)r_2(u,v)}.                   \tag{28}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(r_1=-D\), formula (16) becomes
\[
A(u,v)=R(u,v)-\frac{K(u)}{D(u,v)}.                             \tag{29}
\]
For \(-1<u<0\), \(-1\leq v\leq1\), one has \(D(u,v)>0\).

The regular term is uniformly bounded after division by \(\sqrt P\): there exists a constant \(C\geq0\) such that
\[
\left|\frac{R(u,v)}{\sqrt{P(u,v)}}\right|\leq C
\quad(-1\leq u\leq0,\ -1\leq v\leq1).                       \tag{30}
\]
Indeed, (20) keeps \(r_2,r_4\) away from zero, \(u-1\) is also away from zero on this rectangle, and (10) gives \(P\geq192\). Thus the function in (30) is continuous on a compact rectangle and is bounded there.

The singular factor may be replaced by its corner value with an error proportional to \(D\):
\[
\left|\frac1{\sqrt{P(u,v)}}-\frac1{\sqrt{338}}\right|
 \leq64D(u,v)                                                 \tag{31}
\]
for \(-1\leq u\leq0\), \(-1\leq v\leq1\). Here
\(P(-1,-1)=338\). To justify (31), (10) shows \(1\leq\sqrt P\leq\sqrt{338}\), and therefore
\[
0\leq\frac1{\sqrt P}-\frac1{\sqrt{338}}
 =\frac{\sqrt{338}-\sqrt P}{\sqrt P\sqrt{338}}
 \leq\sqrt{338}-\sqrt P
 \leq338-P.
\]
Expanding (5) and (27), and using \((-u)(v+1)\geq0\), gives
\(338-P(u,v)\leq64D(u,v)\), proving (31).

For \(-1<u<0\), define the boundary integrand corresponding to \(u=\cos a\):
\[
F(u,y)=-\frac{A(u,\cos y)\sqrt{1-u^2}}
 {\sqrt{P(u,\cos y)}}.                                       \tag{32}
\]
From (29), the triangle inequality, (30), and (31), we get pointwise
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigg|F(u,y)&-
 \frac{K(u)}{\sqrt{338}}\sqrt{1-u^2}\, rac1{D(u,\cos y)}\bigg|\\
&\leq \sqrt{1-u^2}\bigl(C+64|K(u)|\bigr).                    \tag{33}
\end{aligned}
\]
The reason the apparent singularity causes no problem in this estimate is that the factor \(D\) in (31) cancels the denominator \(D\) in (29).

It remains to compute the mass of the kernel \(1/D\). We use the elementary cosine-kernel integral
\[
\int_0^\pi\frac{dy}{1-q\cos y}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{1-q^2}}
\qquad(|q|<1).                                                \tag{34}
\]
One proof is to expand the denominator as the uniformly dominated geometric series
\(\sum_{m\geq0}q^m\cos^m y\), integrate term by term, discard the odd moments, and use (1) and (3) on the even moments.

For \(-1<u<0\), take
\[
q=-\frac{1-u}{u+3};
\]
then \(|q|<1\), and
\[
D(u,\cos y)=(u+3)(1-q\cos y).
\]
Formula (34) therefore gives
\[
\int_0^\pi\frac{dy}{D(u,\cos y)}
 =\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{8(u+1)}}.                                 \tag{35}
\]
Indeed,
\((u+3)^2-(1-u)^2=8(u+1)\). Multiplying (35) by
\(\sqrt{1-u^2}\), and using \(1-u^2=(1-u)(1+u)\), yields
\[
\sqrt{1-u^2}\int_0^\pi\frac{dy}{D(u,\cos y)}
 =\pi\sqrt{\frac{1-u}{8}}.                                  \tag{36}
\]

Integrating (33) over \([0,\pi]\) and applying (36), we conclude that
\[
\left|\int_0^\pi F(u,y)\,dy-M(u)\right|
 \leq\pi\sqrt{1-u^2}\bigl(C+64|K(u)|\bigr),                  \tag{37}
\]
where
\[
M(u)=\frac{K(u)\pi}{\sqrt{338}}\sqrt{\frac{1-u}{8}}.          \tag{38}
\]
As \(u\downarrow-1\),
\[
K(u)\longrightarrow K(-1)
 =\frac{770(-26)}{-2}=10010,
\]
and hence
\[
M(u)\longrightarrow
 \frac{10010\pi}{\sqrt{338}}\sqrt{\frac{2}{8}}
 =\frac{5005\pi}{\sqrt{338}}.                               \tag{39}
\]
The right side of (37) tends to zero: \(K(u)\) remains bounded near \(-1\), while \(\sqrt{1-u^2}\to0\). Consequently
\[
\lim_{u\downarrow-1}\int_0^\pi F(u,y)\,dy
 =\frac{5005\pi}{\sqrt{338}}.                               \tag{40}
\]

Now choose any sequence \(u_m\in(-1,0)\) tending to \(-1\), for example
\[
u_m=-1+\frac1{m+1},
\]
and set \(a_m=\arccos u_m\). Then \(a_m\uparrow\pi\),
\(\cos a_m=u_m\), and \(\sin a_m=\sqrt{1-u_m^2}\). Thus the boundary flux in (26) is exactly
\[
\Phi_U(a_m,y)=F(u_m,y).
\]
The function \(I\) is continuous on the full square by (10), so its integrals over \([0,a_m]\times[0,\pi]\) converge to its integral over \([0,\pi]^2\). Passing to the limit in (26) and using (40) gives
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\int_0^\pi\!\int_0^\pi I(x,y)\,dy\,dx
 =\frac{5005\pi}{\sqrt{338}}.}                              \tag{41}
\]

## 5. Completion of the evaluation

Substitute (41) into (14):
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty t_n
 =\frac{\sqrt{392}}{\pi^2}\frac{5005\pi}{\sqrt{338}}
 =\frac{5005}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{392}{338}}.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{392}{338}=\frac{196}{169}=\left(\frac{14}{13}\right)^2

a​nd the square roots are positive,
\[
5005\sqrt{\frac{392}{338}}
 =5005\cdot\frac{14}{13}=5390.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
\frac{4290n+367}{3136^n}\binom{2n}{n}
T_n(14,1)T_n(17,16)=\frac{5390}{\pi}.}
\]
